events.title: Bacon's Rebellion Burns Jamestown
events.blurb: A Virginia planter named Nathaniel Bacon rallied a mixed force of frontier settlers, indentured servants, and enslaved Africans against the colonial governor and marched on the capital, burning Jamestown to the ground. The uprising — the largest armed revolt in colonial America before the Revolution — exposed deep class and racial tensions that led planters to harden the legal distinction between Black slaves and white laborers.
events.revealBlurb: September 19, 1676 — Jamestown, Virginia. Bacon died of dysentery six weeks after burning the capital, ending the rebellion without a battle. Historians argue his multiracial army scared Virginia's elite so badly they accelerated the shift to race-based chattel slavery.

events.title: Declaration of Independence Adopted
events.blurb: Delegates from thirteen British colonies voted to ratify a document asserting that all men are created equal and endowed with unalienable rights, formally severing political ties with the Crown. The declaration listed 27 specific grievances against the king; most delegates signed an engrossed parchment copy nearly a month later.
events.revealBlurb: July 4, 1776 — Philadelphia. Only two men actually signed on the Fourth (Hancock and Thomson). Jefferson, Franklin, and Adams all died on July 4 — Jefferson and Adams on the same day, the 50th anniversary, within hours of each other.

events.title: Missouri Compromise Signed
events.blurb: President James Monroe signed legislation admitting Missouri as a slave state and Maine as a free state simultaneously, preserving the Senate balance between slave and free states, and drawing an invisible line across the continent at latitude 36°30' north — prohibiting slavery in all remaining territory of the Louisiana Purchase above that line.
events.revealBlurb: March 6, 1820 — Washington, D.C. Thomas Jefferson, then 76, called the Missouri debate "a fire bell in the night" that terrified him. The 36°30' line held for 34 years before the Kansas-Nebraska Act erased it in 1854.

events.title: Battle of Gettysburg Begins
events.blurb: Confederate soldiers advancing through a Pennsylvania town accidentally encountered Union cavalry, triggering three days of fighting that became the bloodiest battle ever fought on American soil. A total of approximately 50,000 soldiers were killed, wounded, or went missing — roughly one in three of all combatants engaged on both sides.

events.title: Spanish-American War Declaration
events.blurb: The United States declared war on Spain following the mysterious explosion of the battleship USS Maine in Havana Harbor and years of lurid coverage of Spanish atrocities in Cuba by the American yellow press. The 114-day conflict ended Spanish colonial rule in Cuba, Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines, and announced the United States as a Pacific and Caribbean imperial power.
events.revealBlurb: April 25, 1898 — Washington, D.C. Theodore Roosevelt resigned as Assistant Secretary of the Navy to lead the volunteer Rough Riders cavalry regiment, charging up San Juan Hill — a battle that took one afternoon and made him president. Secretary of State John Hay called it "a splendid little war."

events.title: First Networked Email
events.blurb: A computer engineer working for a Cambridge, Massachusetts research firm sent an electronic message between two computers sitting next to each other in his office, using a symbol from the typewriter keyboard he'd picked precisely because it was never used in names — the "at" sign — to separate the user name from the host machine name. He could not recall years later what the message had contained; probably "QWERTYUIOP" or similar.
events.revealBlurb: October 1971 — Ray Tomlinson at BBN Technologies. The @ symbol's adoption was arbitrary but lasting. Tomlinson's contribution is the reason your email address contains an @. He died in 2016.

events.title: World Wide Web Proposed
events.blurb: A British software engineer working at a Swiss particle-physics laboratory circulated an internal memo proposing a distributed hypertext information management system that would link documents across different computers. His supervisor scribbled "Vague, but exciting" across the top and approved further work. The project would take two more years to become a working system.
events.revealBlurb: March 12, 1989 — Tim Berners-Lee at CERN. His supervisor was Mike Sendall. Berners-Lee never sought patents on his web protocols; he believed the only way they'd spread was to give them away. Queen Elizabeth II knighted him in 2004.

events.title: Amazon Founded
events.blurb: A former hedge-fund vice-president who had driven across the country from New York to Seattle with his wife, writing a business plan on the way, incorporated an online book retailer in the garage of a rented house in a Seattle suburb. He had chosen books because no single physical store could stock every book in print, but one big warehouse could. The company's first website was clunky; the logic was unstoppable.
events.revealBlurb: July 5, 1994 — Jeff Bezos. The company was originally called Cadabra; Bezos changed it after a lawyer misheard it as "cadaver." He considered and rejected relentless.com (now redirecting to Amazon).

events.title: Facebook Buys WhatsApp
events.blurb: A Silicon Valley social-networking giant announced an agreement to acquire a five-year-old messaging app with 450 million users for $19 billion in cash and stock — the largest venture-backed acquisition in tech history. The app had 55 employees; one of its two founders had been rejected when he applied for a job at Facebook eight years earlier.
events.revealBlurb: February 19, 2014 — Facebook buys WhatsApp; co-founders Jan Koum and Brian Acton. The service had been run on the principle of no ads, no gimmicks; Acton later left Facebook over disagreements about monetization and funded the rival Signal.

events.title: Pokémon Go Released
events.blurb: A free mobile game combining augmented reality with a beloved monster-catching franchise launched initially in Australia, New Zealand, and the United States. Within a week, 21 million daily active users were wandering streets and parks staring at their phones, discovering virtual creatures superimposed on physical landmarks. It became the fastest mobile game to reach $500 million in revenue and, more strikingly, got millions of sedentary users to walk outside.
events.revealBlurb: July 6, 2016 — Niantic Inc. Within weeks, fatal accidents, trespassing incidents, and a small bump in physical activity had all been documented. The Pokémon Go wedding, held in New York's Central Park, was among the odder cultural moments of mid-2016.

events.title: First Academy Awards
events.blurb: A 15-minute banquet at a Hollywood hotel awarded twelve statuettes — a 34 cm tall gilded figure of a knight standing on a reel of film — to films, actors, directors, and technicians selected by the newly formed Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences. 270 people attended. The winners had been announced three months earlier. The whole ceremony received brief mention in the next day's Los Angeles Times, on page 10.
events.revealBlurb: May 16, 1929 — Hollywood Roosevelt Hotel. First Best Picture: "Wings." Best Actor: Emil Jannings. The bronze statuette's nickname, "Oscar," was supposedly coined by an Academy librarian who thought it resembled her Uncle Oscar; the story is almost certainly retrofitted.

events.title: Citizen Kane Released
events.blurb: A 25-year-old radio and theatre prodigy made his feature film directing debut with a quasi-biographical study of a newspaper tycoon, structurally organized as a series of flashback interviews about the man's last word ("Rosebud"). The film used deep-focus cinematography, low-angle setups, overlapping dialogue, and non-linear structure in ways that rewrote the cinematic grammar of the next 70 years. Its real-life subject, a media baron, tried to have every print destroyed.
events.revealBlurb: May 1, 1941 — Orson Welles, age 25. The target was William Randolph Hearst, who banned mention of the film in his newspapers. It lost Best Picture to "How Green Was My Valley." It tops nearly every "greatest films of all time" list.

events.title: Bicycle Thieves Released
events.blurb: An Italian director released a quiet 89-minute film about an unemployed working-class man whose stolen bicycle means he cannot take a new job pasting posters on walls. The non-professional actors, documentary-style camera, and refusal of melodramatic conventions defined the Italian neorealist movement. The film spoke for a generation of post-war European audiences who had had enough of Hollywood glamour.
events.revealBlurb: November 24, 1948 — Vittorio De Sica. The father was played by a real factory worker; the son by a young boy De Sica spotted on the street. It won an honorary Academy Award before the foreign language category existed. Its influence on later directors — from Ken Loach to Satyajit Ray — is enormous.

events.title: Back to the Future Released
events.blurb: A 33-year-old director released a 116-minute time-travel comedy about a teenager who accidentally travels 30 years into his own past and must ensure his parents fall in love so he himself will exist. The original cast had been halfway through shooting with a different lead actor when the director fired him and reshot the entire film with a new star. The resulting product became the top-grossing film of its year and spawned two sequels.
events.revealBlurb: July 3, 1985 — Robert Zemeckis, starring Michael J. Fox and Christopher Lloyd. The original Marty was Eric Stoltz; replacing him cost $4 million in reshoots. The DeLorean was Zemeckis's choice — he wanted a time machine that looked, plausibly, like a spaceship.

events.title: Moonlight/La La Land Envelope Mix-Up
events.blurb: At a televised U.S. film industry awards ceremony, presenters opened the wrong envelope and declared a popular musical romance the Best Picture winner. Its producers took the stage, began delivering speeches, and accepted their statuettes before an increasingly visible commotion behind them revealed the mistake. The actual winner was announced with two minutes of live-broadcast awkwardness remaining. It was the first Best Picture with an all-Black cast.
events.revealBlurb: February 26, 2017 — Moonlight, directed by Barry Jenkins. Warren Beatty and Faye Dunaway had been handed the wrong envelope. Jenkins later said: "I saw the envelope. I know what I saw." The accounting firm PwC, responsible for the envelopes, took the blame.

events.title: Sputnik 1 Orbital Launch
events.blurb: A polished aluminum sphere the size of a beach ball lifted off from a steppe launch site and became the first human-made object to orbit Earth. Weighing 83 kilograms and trailing four whip antennas, it circled the planet every 96 minutes and broadcast a radio beep on 20 and 40 MHz audible to amateur operators worldwide for 22 days until its batteries died.
events.revealBlurb: October 4, 1957 — Sputnik 1. It carried zero scientific instruments; the entire payload was a thermometer and a radio transmitter. The beep's rhythm changed with cabin temperature, which meant the world's most-tracked signal was also the world's first space weather report.

events.title: Apollo–Soyuz Handshake in Space
events.blurb: An American Apollo Command Module and a Soviet Soyuz spacecraft docked 225 km above the Atlantic Ocean, and their commanders exchanged the first international handshake in space through a specially built docking adapter module. The joint mission conducted five docking and undocking maneuvers and shared four crew transfer sessions over two days.
events.revealBlurb: July 17, 1975 — Apollo–Soyuz. Stafford and Leonov — who had made the first spacewalk a decade earlier — greeted each other in each other's languages. The crews exchanged seeds, flags, and medals. This was the last flight of an Apollo spacecraft and the last US human spaceflight for six years, until STS-1 in 1981.

events.title: Sojourner Mars Rover Landing
events.blurb: Mars Pathfinder landed on the Ares Vallis flood plain using airbag cushioning, bouncing 15 times before rolling to a stop, and deployed a 10.5 kg six-wheeled rover named Sojourner — the first wheeled vehicle to operate on another planet. Over 83 Martian days the rover analyzed the chemical composition of 16 rock targets, including samples scientists nicknamed Barnacle Bill and Yogi.
events.revealBlurb: July 4, 1997 — Mars Pathfinder. Sojourner was designed for a 7-sol mission and lasted 83. It could fit on a kitchen counter. Mission scientists named rocks after cartoon and pop-culture characters; one rock was called "Casper" because it appeared strangely bright. The rover traveled just 100 meters total — less than a city block.

events.title: Mir Space Station Deorbit
events.blurb: Russia deliberately deorbited the Mir space station after 15 years of continuous operation, using three burns from a docked Progress cargo spacecraft to lower its orbit until it reentered the atmosphere over the South Pacific. Most of the station burned up during reentry, but approximately 1,500 kg of debris survived and splashed into the ocean between Australia and Chile.
events.revealBlurb: March 23, 2001 — Mir deorbit. Mir had been in orbit so long that cosmonauts reported the walls were alive with mold. A Russian company sold pay-per-view rights to watch the reentry from a chartered aircraft. Japan offered to purchase and keep the station operational; the deal fell through over cost. It had been visited by 104 cosmonauts and astronauts from 12 nations.

events.title: Cassini Enters Saturn Orbit
events.blurb: The Cassini–Huygens spacecraft fired its main engine for 96 minutes to decelerate into Saturn orbit, threading a gap between the planet's F and G rings — a maneuver so precisely executed that the trajectory team reported it arrived within one kilometer of the planned position. Cassini became the first spacecraft to orbit Saturn, beginning a 13-year study of the planet and its moons.
events.revealBlurb: July 1, 2004 — Cassini. Six months later, Cassini released the Huygens probe, which descended through Titan's atmosphere and transmitted data from its surface — the most distant landing ever achieved at the time. Cassini ultimately discovered that Enceladus has active geysers of water vapor, making it one of the top candidates for extraterrestrial life.

events.title: Bach Dedicates Brandenburg Concertos
events.blurb: A 36-year-old German court composer, looking for a new job, sent a margrave a set of six concerto grossi he had been accumulating over several years. The dedication was effusive; he apologized for the "vast distance between his person and the margrave." The margrave never acknowledged the gift, let alone hired him, and probably never had them performed. The manuscripts sat in a Prussian archive for 128 years before rediscovery.
events.revealBlurb: March 24, 1721 — Johann Sebastian Bach, addressing Christian Ludwig of Brandenburg. The scores were narrowly rescued from Allied bombing in 1945. The music now exists thanks to a librarian who grabbed them as he fled Leipzig for the Harz mountains.

events.title: The Rite of Spring Riot
events.blurb: A 30-year-old Russian composer's ballet score, depicting a pagan spring ritual with jagged rhythms, dissonant chord stacks, and primitivist choreography, premiered at a new Paris theatre and nearly caused a full-scale audience riot. Shouts, whistles, and fistfights broke out within minutes; the choreographer had to shout counts to dancers from the wings because they couldn't hear the orchestra. The piece is now considered one of the pivotal works of 20th-century music.
events.revealBlurb: May 29, 1913 — Igor Stravinsky and Ballets Russes at Théâtre des Champs-Élysées, Paris. Choreography by Vaslav Nijinsky. The Parisian critic Carl Van Vechten reported his seat-neighbour beating rhythmically on his head with his fists in distress.

events.title: Elvis Records "That's All Right"
events.blurb: During a break in a fruitless recording session in Memphis, a 19-year-old truck driver began playing an uptempo blues song with such energy that the studio owner halted the session, rewound the tape, and asked him to do it again from the start. The recording blended country and rhythm-and-blues in a style that had no existing commercial category.

events.title: Elvis's First Sun Session
events.blurb: A 19-year-old truck driver who had walked into a small Memphis recording studio a year earlier to make an acetate for his mother's birthday showed up for a late-night try-out with two local session musicians. The session was going nowhere until, during a break, the kid started goofing around with an old R&B song by Arthur Crudup. The engineer slapped the tape on and caught it. Within weeks the song was a regional hit.
events.revealBlurb: July 5, 1954 — Elvis Presley, Scotty Moore, and Bill Black at Sun Records, Memphis. The song was "That's All Right (Mama)." Studio owner Sam Phillips had famously said he could make "a billion dollars" if he could find a white man who sang with a Black feel.

events.title: Woodstock Festival
events.blurb: A three-day music festival, overcapacity within hours of opening, drew an estimated 400,000 young people to a dairy farm in upstate New York despite severe rain. Fences collapsed; the event became de facto free. 32 acts performed — Jimi Hendrix, Janis Joplin, The Who, Santana, Creedence Clearwater Revival, Joan Baez. Two people died (one from an overdose, one crushed by a tractor); two babies were born. The festival became the defining symbol of the 1960s counterculture.
events.revealBlurb: August 15-18, 1969 — on Max Yasgur's farm in Bethel, NY. Hendrix closed at 9 AM Monday morning to a dwindling crowd with a distorted, feedback-laced "Star-Spangled Banner." The 1970 documentary won an Oscar.

events.title: Spinning Jenny Patented
events.blurb: A textile worker patented a multi-spindle spinning frame that allowed a single operator to spin eight threads simultaneously — a number later increased to 120. The machine slashed the cost of cotton yarn and displaced the hand-spinning cottage industry within a generation.

events.title: Cotton Gin Patented
events.blurb: A 28-year-old Yale-educated New Englander, tutoring at a Georgia plantation, built a simple wooden cylinder with wire teeth that combed cotton seeds out of fibres 50 times faster than a slave's fingers could. He patented the device. Rather than being royally enriched, he spent years litigating piracy; the design was too simple to protect. The invention made short-staple cotton profitable across the American South, entrenching slavery economically just as it was weakening elsewhere.
events.revealBlurb: March 14, 1794 — Eli Whitney. He later pivoted to manufacturing muskets with interchangeable parts — an innovation that shaped the later assembly-line system. Demand for enslaved labour in the Deep South grew enormously between 1790 and 1860, in large part because of the gin.

events.title: Edison's Practical Lightbulb
events.blurb: After 14 months of systematic experimentation with thousands of possible filament materials — and many previous lightbulb designs by other inventors — an American inventor's laboratory team achieved a 40-hour burn using a carbonized cotton-thread filament in an evacuated glass bulb. The achievement's significance was not inventing the lightbulb itself (which had existed in various forms for decades) but making one that burned long enough to be commercially viable.
events.revealBlurb: October 21, 1879 — Thomas Edison at Menlo Park. His 1880 improved version used a bamboo filament and burned 1,200 hours. Edison's real genius was less invention than the systematic industrial R&D lab he created — the template for every modern corporate research operation.

events.title: Homestead Strike
events.blurb: A Pennsylvania steelworkers' strike against wage cuts at a mill owned by a famous industrialist turned into a gun battle after management hired 300 Pinkerton private detectives to escort strike-breakers into the plant. The Pinkertons arrived by barge up the Monongahela River before dawn; strikers and their families met them on the banks with rifles. Nine strikers and seven Pinkertons died in the all-day firefight. The state militia restored order; the union was broken; US steelworkers remained largely non-unionized for 45 years.
events.revealBlurb: July 6, 1892 — Homestead Steel Works, owned by Andrew Carnegie, managed during the strike by Henry Clay Frick. Frick survived an assassination attempt by anarchist Alexander Berkman three weeks later, shot and stabbed multiple times but recovered. Carnegie was in Scotland when the violence occurred.

events.title: Wright Brothers' First Flight
events.blurb: Two American bicycle-shop owners from Dayton, Ohio achieved the first sustained, controlled, powered flight of a heavier-than-air aircraft on a windswept dune at the Outer Banks of North Carolina. The first flight lasted 12 seconds and covered 36 metres — about the wingspan of a modern commercial airliner. They made three more flights that morning; the fourth covered 260 metres in 59 seconds. Few newspapers reported the achievement; commercial aviation took another three decades to arrive.
events.revealBlurb: December 17, 1903 — Orville and Wilbur Wright at Kill Devil Hills, near Kitty Hawk, NC. The flyer is now in the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum. The pair spent 4 years after their first flight battling patent disputes and litigation rather than manufacturing planes.

events.title: Galileo Observes the Moon Through a Telescope
events.blurb: Turning a new optical instrument toward the night sky, an Italian mathematician observed that the Moon's surface was rough, mountainous, and marked by craters — directly contradicting the ancient belief that celestial bodies were perfect smooth spheres. Careful drawings of the shadow lines allowed him to estimate the height of lunar mountains by triangulating shadow lengths.
events.revealBlurb: November 30, 1609 — Galileo had only heard a description of a Dutch spyglass and built his own without ever seeing one. His 1610 pamphlet Sidereus Nuncius went through its entire print run within a week. He dedicated Jupiter's four moons to the Medici family to secure patronage — an early example of branded science.

events.title: Kepler's Laws of Planetary Motion Published
events.blurb: A German mathematician published two laws describing how planets orbit the Sun: first, that orbits are ellipses with the Sun at one focus; second, that a line from the planet to the Sun sweeps equal areas in equal times — meaning planets move faster when close to the Sun. A third law, relating orbital period to distance, followed ten years later, providing the first precise mathematical description of the solar system.
events.revealBlurb: 1609 (laws 1&2) and 1619 (law 3) — Johannes Kepler derived the laws from the most precise observational data in the world, collected by Tycho Brahe. Brahe had guarded the data obsessively and refused to share it; Kepler obtained it only after Brahe's sudden death. He later calculated that Brahe may have died from a burst bladder after refusing to leave a banquet to use the lavatory.

events.title: Endosymbiotic Theory Published
events.blurb: A paper proposed that the energy-producing mitochondria and photosynthetic chloroplasts inside complex cells were originally free-living bacteria that had been engulfed by a host cell and retained over billions of years — a radical claim that the cell's most vital structures were once independent organisms. The paper had been rejected by approximately fifteen journals before finding a publisher.
events.revealBlurb: June 1967 — Lynn Margulis submitted the paper under her married surname Sagan; it became one of biology's most-cited papers after decades of derision. Her critics called it "too fantastic." When the hypothesis was tested by comparing DNA in mitochondria to bacterial DNA in the 1980s, it matched almost exactly.

events.title: Higgs Boson Announced
events.blurb: At a packed seminar, two independent experimental teams working at the world's largest particle accelerator announced the observation of a new particle consistent with the long-predicted Higgs boson — the quantum field excitation that gives other fundamental particles their mass. The discovery completed the standard model of particle physics, confirming a prediction made nearly fifty years earlier.
events.revealBlurb: July 4, 2012 — Peter Higgs, who had predicted the boson in 1964, was in the audience and reportedly wept. The two experiments — ATLAS and CMS — had been run in blind competition to avoid bias. Higgs and François Englert shared the Nobel Prize in Physics the following year.

events.title: First Black Hole Image Captured
events.blurb: A global network of radio telescopes, coordinated to act as a single Earth-sized dish, produced the first direct image of a black hole's event horizon — a glowing ring of superheated gas surrounding a dark central void at the centre of a galaxy 55 million light-years away. Processing the petabytes of data required a custom algorithm developed in part by a graduate student whose contribution went initially unrecognised.
events.revealBlurb: April 10, 2019 — the black hole in galaxy M87 is 6.5 billion times the mass of the Sun. Katie Bouman, then a postdoc, developed much of the imaging algorithm and became briefly internet-famous when a photo of her looking at the result on a laptop went viral. The press release was coordinated across six cities in six time zones simultaneously.

events.title: Hands Across America
events.blurb: Around 6.5 million Americans paid $10 each to stand along a 6,754-kilometre line stretching from a California beach to a New York skyscraper, holding hands for fifteen minutes as part of a charity event to raise money for hunger and homelessness relief. The line required one person every 0.77 metres; roughly half the route was inhabited uninterrupted, the rest had gaps. The event raised $34 million after expenses and was widely considered more spectacle than effective philanthropy.
events.revealBlurb: May 25, 1986 — organized by USA for Africa. The line ran from the Santa Monica Pier to the Battery in Manhattan via 16 states and DC. A theme song was recorded by over 500 celebrities. The event inspired the 2019 horror film "Us," where the hand-holding line takes on sinister significance.

events.title: Seinfeld Premieres
events.blurb: A 90-minute pilot episode titled "The Seinfeld Chronicles" aired on NBC, starring a 35-year-old New York stand-up comedian as a fictionalized version of himself and three friends navigating petty social minutiae in Manhattan. NBC had almost dropped the show; test audiences had responded coolly. A show famously about "nothing," it would run 180 episodes over nine seasons and become one of the most influential sitcoms in television history.
events.revealBlurb: July 5, 1989 — Jerry Seinfeld, Jason Alexander, Michael Richards (Julia Louis-Dreyfus joined season 2). Co-creator Larry David later made Curb Your Enthusiasm, essentially a Seinfeld-universe spinoff. The cast famously turned down $5 million per episode each to continue past season 9.

events.title: O.J. Simpson Bronco Chase
events.blurb: A 46-year-old former football star, charged with the murders of his ex-wife and her friend, failed to surrender to police at the agreed time. A friend drove him along a Los Angeles freeway in a white Ford Bronco at around 55 km/h, pursued by police cruisers and a dozen news helicopters. An estimated 95 million Americans watched the chase live on television. It ended with his surrender at his home.
events.revealBlurb: June 17, 1994 — O.J. Simpson, driver Al Cowlings. NBC interrupted Game 5 of the NBA Finals between the Knicks and Rockets to show the chase. Simpson was acquitted of murder on October 3, 1995 in what was nicknamed the "Trial of the Century."

events.title: Spice Girls' "Wannabe"
events.blurb: A British pop group of five young women released their debut single — a bouncy three-minute track with a rap-like opening, shot on a single take in a Lisbon hotel — hit number one in 37 countries over the following months. The five — styled "Scary," "Sporty," "Baby," "Ginger," and "Posh" — would dominate late-1990s pop culture with a "Girl Power" message that was earnest, commercial, and enormously successful. They sold 100 million records globally.
events.revealBlurb: July 8, 1996 — Spice Girls: Melanie B (Scary), Melanie C (Sporty), Emma Bunton (Baby), Geri Halliwell (Ginger), Victoria Adams (Posh). The video was shot in a single day at the Hotel Palácio in Portugal. Victoria Beckham married David Beckham in 1999; she launched a fashion career later.

events.title: Titanic Released
events.blurb: A Canadian director released a 195-minute romantic epic about a fictional couple aboard the 1912 maiden voyage of the British ocean liner. The production had been the most expensive in Hollywood history, its budget having doubled during filming; industry wags predicted financial disaster. The film ran in theatres for ten months, won 11 Oscars, and became the first film to gross over a billion dollars. Its director famously shouted "I'm king of the world" from the podium.
events.revealBlurb: December 19, 1997 — James Cameron, starring Leonardo DiCaprio and Kate Winslet. It grossed $2.2 billion; Cameron's subsequent "Avatar" beat it 12 years later, also directed by him. Celine Dion's "My Heart Will Go On" spent three weeks at #1.

events.title: Michelangelo's David Unveiled
events.blurb: A 29-year-old Florentine sculptor unveiled a 5.17-metre marble nude of a biblical hero, carved over three years from a single block of Carrara marble that had been rejected by two earlier sculptors as flawed. The statue was intended for the rooftop of a cathedral; a committee that included Leonardo da Vinci decided the work was too significant to put out of sight and instead installed it in the main square of the city.
events.revealBlurb: September 8, 1504 — Michelangelo Buonarroti. Moving it from the workshop to the Piazza della Signoria took 40 men 4 days. The statue was damaged by a mob in 1527 and by a 1991 attack with a hammer; it now stands indoors at the Accademia, where a copy watches over the piazza.

events.title: Raphael's School of Athens
events.blurb: A 28-year-old Umbrian painter completed the second of four monumental frescoes on the walls of the pope's private library at the Vatican, gathering the giants of classical philosophy into a single imaginary architectural space. Plato and Aristotle walk forward from a vanishing point; Pythagoras writes in a book, Euclid draws on a slate, Heraclitus leans alone on a block. The face of Euclid is the architect Bramante; Heraclitus is Michelangelo, working bitterly next door.
events.revealBlurb: 1511 — Raphael Sanzio, in the Stanza della Segnatura. The rivalry with Michelangelo, then painting the Sistine Ceiling a short walk away, was real; Raphael added him as an afterthought in a late revision.

events.title: Rembrandt's Night Watch
events.blurb: A 36-year-old Dutch painter completed a 3.6 by 4.4 metre group portrait of an Amsterdam militia company, commissioned by 18 civic-guard officers each paying 100 guilders for his place. Unlike the static lineup portraits typical of the genre, the painter depicted the company in motion, emerging from a shadowed arch with a drum rolling and a musket firing. The title "Night Watch" is a misnomer added by 19th-century curators; varnish had darkened a daytime scene.
events.revealBlurb: 1642 — Rembrandt van Rijn. Now in Amsterdam's Rijksmuseum. It was trimmed on all sides in 1715 to fit between two doorways, losing two figures. A recent 8K restoration reconstructed the missing pieces using AI.

events.title: Velázquez's Las Meninas
events.blurb: A court painter completed a 3.2-metre oil depicting a 5-year-old Spanish princess surrounded by her ladies-in-waiting, two dwarfs, a dog, and — impossibly — himself at his easel. A distant mirror on the back wall reflects the figures of her parents, the king and queen, who appear to be standing exactly where the viewer stands. The painting is essentially a visual puzzle about who is depicting whom and from where.
events.revealBlurb: 1656 — Diego Velázquez at the Spanish court. The princess is Margarita Teresa. Now in Madrid's Prado. Picasso painted 58 variations on it in 1957. Foucault opened his book The Order of Things with a long reading of its perspective.

events.title: Banksy Shreds at Auction
events.blurb: A framed spray-painting of a girl releasing a heart-shaped balloon, sold at a London auction for £1.04 million ten seconds earlier, began to buzz mechanically and slid partway through a concealed shredder built into the custom frame. Half the canvas emerged in vertical strips; the auction house staff stared; the hammer had already fallen. The anonymous street artist who had built the device posted a video saying the mechanism was supposed to shred the whole picture.
events.revealBlurb: October 5, 2018 — Banksy, at Sotheby's London. The buyer honored the purchase. The half-shredded work was retitled "Love is in the Bin" and resold three years later for £18.6 million — 18 times the original price.

events.title: Battle of Britain
events.blurb: For nearly four months, an island nation's outnumbered fighter force faced daily mass raids by the world's most battle-hardened air force, with the explicit goal of destroying aerial defences so that a seaborne invasion could follow. Radar stations, sector control rooms, and the pilots' ability to keep flying became the three fulcrums on which the outcome balanced.
events.revealBlurb: July 10 – October 31, 1940. The RAF lost 1,023 aircraft; the Luftwaffe lost 1,887. Churchill's "The Few" speech on August 20 honoured the pilots — the average age of whom was just 20. Germany quietly postponed its invasion plan on September 17 and never rescheduled it.

events.title: Enigma Broken at Bletchley
events.blurb: A team of mathematicians and linguists working in a cluttered hut in the English countryside deployed an electromechanical machine that could test thousands of rotor settings per minute, cracking the daily-changed cipher used by an opposing military's command and logistics networks — and began reading intercepted messages within hours of their transmission.
events.revealBlurb: May 1940 — Bletchley Park's upgraded Bombe, designed by Alan Turing and Gordon Welchman, began breaking Luftwaffe "Red" traffic daily. The secret was so tightly held that some commanders were fed cover stories about lucky reconnaissance flights. The intelligence was codenamed Ultra and arguably shortened the conflict by two years.

events.title: Japanese-American Internment
events.blurb: A presidential order authorised the forced removal of all people of a specific ethnic ancestry from the entire western coast of a country — regardless of citizenship — to inland camps surrounded by guard towers and barbed wire, without trial or individual evidence of wrongdoing. Roughly 122,000 people were displaced; two-thirds were native-born citizens.
events.revealBlurb: Executive Order 9066, signed February 19, 1942. The Supreme Court upheld it in 1944. In 1988, Congress formally apologised and paid $20,000 in reparations to each surviving detainee — roughly 82,000 people. A 2011 Department of Justice memo officially acknowledged the government's lawyers had hidden evidence of innocence from the original court.

events.title: Dieppe Raid
events.blurb: Roughly 6,000 troops — mostly Canadians — landed in daylight on a heavily defended beach overlooked by cliffs and were cut down before many could clear the waterline, suffering nearly 60 percent casualties in under ten hours. Planners later claimed the catastrophic failure provided lessons that saved countless lives in subsequent amphibious operations.
events.revealBlurb: August 19, 1942 — Operation Jubilee. Of 4,963 Canadians who embarked, only 2,210 returned to England; 907 were killed and 1,946 taken prisoner. The Germans, who had received advance intelligence, held their positions with minimal effort. Churchill admitted privately it was "a very heavy and grievous loss."

events.title: Battle of Kursk
events.blurb: Two million soldiers and nearly 6,000 tanks clashed around a salient in the steppe, with the attackers driving into prepared defences twelve layers deep that had been built specifically to absorb and exhaust an armoured offensive. For the first time in the eastern conflict, a major German armoured attack was stopped before achieving a breakthrough.
events.revealBlurb: July 5 – August 23, 1943. The Germans had repeatedly delayed the offensive to wait for newer tanks, giving Soviet intelligence — fed by the British Ultra intercepts — five months to prepare. The opening day, July 5, was the single costliest day in the history of aerial warfare by aircraft lost. Germany never regained strategic initiative in the East afterward.

events.title: Battle of Tours
events.blurb: A Frankish mayor of the palace led an infantry army into a defensive wall of shields against a much larger Umayyad cavalry force that had been raiding deep into western Europe. The battle's outcome stopped the northward expansion of the Islamic caliphate into the Frankish heartland and established the Carolingian dynasty as the dominant power of the region.
events.revealBlurb: October 10, 732 — Charles Martel ("Charles the Hammer") in central France. His grandson Charlemagne would be crowned emperor 68 years later. Edward Gibbon later wrote that without the victory, "the interpretation of the Koran would now be taught in the schools of Oxford."

events.title: Charlemagne Crowned Emperor
events.blurb: A Frankish king, in a papal basilica in the old western imperial capital for Christmas Mass, rose from prayer to be unexpectedly crowned "Emperor of the Romans" by the pope. The coronation resurrected, at least in title, a western empire that had been extinct for 324 years, and established a relationship between popes and emperors that would shape European politics for eight centuries.
events.revealBlurb: December 25, 800 — Charlemagne in Rome, crowned by Pope Leo III. Charlemagne later claimed he had been surprised — but the pope probably wouldn't have dared without his consent. The Holy Roman Empire survived in one form or another until 1806.

events.title: Great Schism of Christianity
events.blurb: The pope's legate and the patriarch of a Bosphorus capital excommunicated each other over a long-brewing dispute about papal authority, the phrasing of the Nicene Creed, and the use of unleavened bread in the Eucharist. Mutual anathemas remained in force for 911 years. The Roman and Orthodox churches have never fully reunited.
events.revealBlurb: July 16, 1054 — Cardinal Humbert and Patriarch Michael Cerularius. The excommunications were formally lifted in 1965 by Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras. The "filioque clause" dispute sounds obscure but was genuinely the trigger.

events.title: Battle of Hastings
events.blurb: A Norman duke from across the English Channel invaded a southern English kingdom with 7,000 men, met its exhausted king — who had marched south after defeating a Norwegian invasion three weeks earlier in the north — on a hillside near the coast, and won in an all-day battle. The English king was killed, reportedly by an arrow through the eye. The victor replaced the Anglo-Saxon aristocracy with his own.
events.revealBlurb: October 14, 1066 — William the Conqueror vs. Harold Godwinson near the town of Battle, East Sussex. The Bayeux Tapestry, a 70-metre embroidered account, was sewn within a decade. Modern English is still 50–60 percent French-derived because of the resulting Norman elite.

events.title: First Crusade Takes Jerusalem
events.blurb: After a month-long siege and a three-year, 3,000-kilometre march from Europe, an army of Frankish knights and footsoldiers breached the walls of a holy city in the Levant and slaughtered its Muslim and Jewish inhabitants indiscriminately over two days — perhaps 30,000 people. The first crusader state was established with a European dynasty on the throne; it would last 88 years.
events.revealBlurb: July 15, 1099 — the siege was broken when two Flemish knights scaled a siege tower onto the wall. The leaders competed to be the first to reach the Holy Sepulchre. Godfrey of Bouillon refused the crown of a city "where his savior had worn a crown of thorns" — he was titled "Defender" instead.

events.title: Parthenon Marbles Completed
events.blurb: Under the direction of a single master sculptor, a team of Athenian craftsmen completed the exterior sculptural programme of a temple on a fortified limestone hill above their city — a continuous carved frieze 160 metres long depicting a civic religious procession, plus 92 metopes and two pediments. The sculptures were painted in vivid colours; the bleached white appearance known to modern viewers is an accident of weathering.
events.revealBlurb: c. 438 BCE — Phidias, chief sculptor of the Parthenon in Athens. Lord Elgin removed about half the surviving marbles between 1801 and 1812 and sold them to the British Museum. Greece has been asking for them back for over 200 years.

events.title: First Impressionist Exhibition
events.blurb: Thirty painters whose work had been repeatedly rejected by the official French Salon rented the studio of a photographer on a Paris boulevard and held their own group show. A review in a satirical magazine mocked one of the paintings — "Impression, Sunrise" — and gave the movement the name it would keep. The show attracted 3,500 visitors, which was dismal; mockery outweighed admiration; most of the painters struggled financially for another decade.
events.revealBlurb: April 15 to May 15, 1874 — 35 Boulevard des Capucines, Paris. Participants included Monet, Renoir, Degas, Pissarro, Cézanne, Berthe Morisot, and Sisley. The critic who coined the term, Louis Leroy, titled his review "Exhibition of the Impressionists" sarcastically; the painters adopted it.

events.title: Munch's The Scream
events.blurb: A 30-year-old Norwegian painter completed the first version of a composition he had been sketching for years, showing a androgynous figure with an egg-shaped face and open mouth on a bridge above a blood-orange sky. The painter later wrote of the walk at dusk during which he had felt "a shriek passing through nature." He produced four versions across several decades; two have been stolen, and both were recovered.
events.revealBlurb: 1893 — Edvard Munch. The sky's colour may be real: it has been linked to the atmospheric effects of the Krakatoa eruption ten years earlier. The Oslo theft in 1994 happened during the opening ceremony of the Winter Olympics. The thieves left a note: "Thanks for the poor security."

events.title: Picasso's Guernica
events.blurb: A Spanish painter in his mid-fifties produced a 3.5-metre-tall monochrome canvas for the Spanish pavilion at a Paris international exposition, depicting the destruction of a Basque town by Nazi and Fascist bombers at the request of the Spanish Nationalist forces a month earlier. Screaming women, a dismembered soldier, a wounded horse, a bull, and a single lightbulb-like eye crowd the picture. The artist refused to have it displayed in his homeland until fascist rule there ended.
events.revealBlurb: Painted January-June 1937; exhibited July 12 at the Paris Exhibition. Picasso. The bombing of Guernica was on April 26, 1937. The painting toured the world for 40 years, then was installed in Madrid in 1981, six years after Franco's death.

events.title: Warhol's Campbell's Soup Cans
events.blurb: A 33-year-old former commercial illustrator exhibited 32 canvases, each showing a single can of condensed soup — one for each of the 32 varieties the food company then sold. He had painted them by projecting photographic images onto the canvas and tracing. The show sold modestly: five of the canvases went for $100 each; the gallery owner bought them back and later resold the whole set for $2 million.
events.revealBlurb: July 9, 1962 — Ferus Gallery, Los Angeles, Andy Warhol. The artist said he ate Campbell's soup every day for 20 years. The set is now in MoMA. Warhol would soon apply the same silk-screen methods to Marilyn Monroe, Jackie Kennedy, and Elvis.

events.title: Hip-Hop Born in the Bronx
events.blurb: An 18-year-old Jamaican-born DJ, using two turntables to extend the instrumental breaks of funk and soul records, played his younger sister's back-to-school party in the rec room of a public housing building in the South Bronx. His technique of looping drum breaks became the foundation of hip-hop. The party went so well that he began DJ-ing at local parks and block parties; rappers (then called MCs) began performing over his sets. A new culture was born.
events.revealBlurb: August 11, 1973 — DJ Kool Herc (Clive Campbell) at 1520 Sedgwick Avenue, the Bronx. The address is now a national historic site. Herc's "merry-go-round" technique of using two copies of the same record to loop the break is still the foundation of every hip-hop DJ set.

events.title: Rapper's Delight Released
events.blurb: Three rappers from the New York metro area, assembled by an independent label, released a 15-minute track over a bassline lifted from a recent disco hit. It was the first hip-hop single to reach the U.S. Billboard Top 40. The culture it came from had been thriving in parks and clubs around the Bronx for six years; this record introduced it to mainstream white America and set rap on the path from subcultural movement to dominant global genre.
events.revealBlurb: September 1979 — Sugarhill Gang on Sugar Hill Records. The bassline was from Chic's "Good Times"; Chic's Nile Rodgers and Bernard Edwards sued and received co-writing credit. The track went platinum in the US and hit #3 in the UK.

events.title: John Lennon Shot
events.blurb: A 40-year-old former Beatle, returning to his Manhattan apartment building with his wife after a late-night recording session, was shot four times in the back at close range by a young man he had signed an autograph for earlier that afternoon. He was pronounced dead at a nearby hospital 20 minutes later. Vigils were held around the world. His wife asked that his birthday be celebrated with international moments of silence, which has since become a yearly tradition.
events.revealBlurb: December 8, 1980 — John Lennon at The Dakota, NYC. Shooter Mark David Chapman remains in prison, denied parole 13 times. Lennon's album "Double Fantasy" had been released three weeks earlier; it took on enormous posthumous sales.

events.title: Live Aid
events.blurb: Two simultaneous 16-hour benefit concerts, one at a stadium in London and one at a stadium in Philadelphia, were broadcast live to an estimated 1.9 billion people in 150 countries — at the time perhaps 40 percent of the world population. The concerts raised around $127 million for Ethiopian famine relief. A British band's 21-minute set, by most accounts, stole the whole day. Its lead singer's synchronized clap-along with 72,000 people is the stuff of legend.
events.revealBlurb: July 13, 1985 — Wembley Stadium and JFK Stadium. The stealing-the-show band was Queen, Freddie Mercury at Wembley. Co-organizers Bob Geldof and Midge Ure. "Feed the World" had been launched by the Band Aid charity single the previous Christmas.

events.title: Spotify Launches
events.blurb: A Swedish music-streaming service, developed in Stockholm and Stockholm alone for two years, launched invitation-only to users in six European countries. The service offered an enormous music library — eventually over 100 million tracks — free with ads or $10/month without. It would restructure the entire music business: album sales collapsed, streaming became the default, and royalties flowed through aggregation models that artists found miserly.
events.revealBlurb: October 7, 2008 — founded by Daniel Ek and Martin Lorentzon. The service arrived in the U.S. in July 2011 after lengthy negotiations with major labels. It had 620 million monthly active users as of 2024 — the largest audio subscription service ever.

events.title: Battles of Lexington and Concord
events.blurb: That spring morning, British regulars marching to seize a colonial weapons cache at Concord, Massachusetts, exchanged fire with local militia at Lexington before the colonists scattered; at Concord's North Bridge, a second volley triggered a running battle that chased the redcoats back to Boston. The day produced roughly 300 total casualties and the phrase "the shot heard round the world."
events.revealBlurb: April 19, 1775 — Lexington and Concord, Massachusetts. Nobody knows who fired first at Lexington — colonial accounts and British accounts flatly contradict each other. The phrase "shot heard round the world" was written by Ralph Waldo Emerson in 1837, over 60 years after the fact.

events.title: British Surrender at Saratoga
events.blurb: A British army of 6,000 men under a genteel general who had marched south from Canada intending to split the American colonies along the Hudson Valley found itself encircled at a rural New York hamlet after two pitched battles and dwindling supplies. The general surrendered his entire force to the American commander. It was the most consequential Allied success of the war; France, which had been secretly aiding the colonies, publicly entered the conflict four months later.
events.revealBlurb: October 17, 1777 — British general John Burgoyne surrenders to American general Horatio Gates. Burgoyne had been marching from Canada; a complementary British push up the Hudson from New York had been misdirected to Pennsylvania. The victory secured French diplomatic recognition and military alliance.

events.title: Storming of the Bastille
events.blurb: A mob of several thousand Parisians, enraged by the dismissal of a popular finance minister and rumours of royal military preparations, stormed a royal fortress prison on the city's eastern edge in search of gunpowder stored there. The garrison surrendered after a bloody four-hour assault; the commandant was murdered and his head carried on a pike through the streets. The prison itself held only seven prisoners. The date became the French national holiday.
events.revealBlurb: July 14, 1789 — the Bastille. Seven prisoners: four forgers, two lunatics, one aristocrat imprisoned by his family. Marquis de Launay, the commandant, is the famous head on the pike. Parisians began demolishing the fortress the next morning; it was fully down within three months.

events.title: Haiti Declares Independence
events.blurb: A former slave turned general, addressing a small crowd at a town on a Caribbean island, declared the independence of a new sovereign state that replaced a French sugar colony. It took the name of the original Taíno indigenous word for the island. It was the first independent state in Latin America, the only one to emerge from a successful slave revolt, and the second republic in the Western hemisphere. European powers reacted with diplomatic ostracism; the United States refused recognition for 58 years.
events.revealBlurb: January 1, 1804 — Jean-Jacques Dessalines at Gonaïves, Haiti. France demanded reparations for "lost property" — 150 million francs — that Haiti finished paying only in 1947. The combination of debt, ostracism, and internal strife has shaped Haitian poverty for two centuries.

events.title: Revolutions of 1848
events.blurb: Political unrest that had been gathering over economic recession and demands for constitutional government erupted within weeks across most of the European continent, beginning with a winter insurrection in Paris that deposed the king. Vienna, Berlin, Milan, Budapest, Prague, and a dozen other capitals followed within months. Liberals, nationalists, socialists, and workers briefly shared rhetoric; conservatives reorganized and, over the following year, crushed nearly every revolt. The conservative order emerged apparently reinforced — but the political grammar of 19th-century Europe had changed.
events.revealBlurb: February-June 1848 — "The Springtime of Nations." Louis-Philippe of France fled in February; Metternich resigned in Vienna in March. Only France produced lasting regime change, and it soon produced Napoleon III's Second Empire. Karl Marx and Engels published the Communist Manifesto that same February.

events.title: American Idol Premieres
events.blurb: A singing-competition reality show — adapted from a British format — premiered on Fox with a caustic British music executive as its lead judge, flanked by two milder American ones. The first season's audition rounds and final contestant-viewer-vote format drew enormous audiences; its first winner, a 20-year-old Texan waitress, became a genuine pop star. The show's stern British judge became a cultural shorthand for merciless critique.
events.revealBlurb: June 11, 2002 — judges Simon Cowell, Paula Abdul, Randy Jackson. Host Ryan Seacrest. Season 1 winner Kelly Clarkson went on to a successful music and TV career. American Idol ran on Fox until 2016 and was revived on ABC in 2018; Clarkson's "A Moment Like This" is still its most famous product.

events.title: Michael Jackson Dies
events.blurb: A 50-year-old American singer widely regarded as the most successful pop star of his generation died of cardiac arrest at his rented Los Angeles home while preparing for a 50-concert comeback tour in London. His personal physician was later convicted of involuntary manslaughter for administering propofol, a surgical anesthetic, to help him sleep. His death prompted an outpouring of grief that crashed major websites and sold over 35 million of his records in the following six months.
events.revealBlurb: June 25, 2009 — Michael Jackson. His physician, Conrad Murray, was sentenced to 4 years and served 2. His public memorial on July 7 drew 31 million U.S. TV viewers. The "This Is It" concert film, compiled from rehearsal footage, grossed $261 million posthumously.

events.title: Gangnam Style Goes Viral
events.blurb: A music video by a 34-year-old South Korean rapper was uploaded to YouTube, featuring a catchy synth-pop track, exaggerated dance moves, and satirical shots of an upscale Seoul district. Within three months the video had 300 million views, passing Justin Bieber's "Baby" as the most-viewed in YouTube history. Within five, it crossed one billion. The horse-riding dance broke through into American late-night comedy, political campaigns, and every wedding reception in the world.
events.revealBlurb: July 15, 2012 — PSY (Park Jae-sang). It held the most-viewed YouTube video title until it was surpassed by "See You Again" in 2017 and then "Despacito." The video's 2014 view count literally broke YouTube's 32-bit counter, requiring an engineering upgrade to 64 bits.

events.title: "The Dress" Goes Viral
events.blurb: A 21-year-old Scottish woman posted a photograph of a dress on her Tumblr account asking for help settling a family argument — was it black and blue, or white and gold? The photo went viral overnight. Approximately 40 percent of viewers saw it as white and gold; 50 percent as black and blue. Vision scientists spent months examining why. The actual dress, in real life, was black and blue. The phenomenon became a landmark case study in how individual visual perception varies based on assumptions about ambient lighting.
events.revealBlurb: February 26, 2015 — Cecilia Bleasdale's photograph, posted by Caitlin McNeill. Roman Originals, who made the dress, saw a 560 percent spike in sales. Neuroscientists published papers on it for years. It revived serious research into color constancy and top-down visual processing.

events.title: Stranger Things Premieres
events.blurb: A supernatural drama set in a small Indiana town in 1983 premiered on Netflix, combining Spielbergian child adventure, Stephen King atmospheric horror, and 80s-movie production design with a pitch-perfect synth-wave score. The 8-episode first season was Netflix's first genuine original-production cultural sensation and proved that the streaming service could create prestige-TV hits without a traditional network. The cast of unknown child actors became overnight celebrities.
events.revealBlurb: July 15, 2016 — Netflix; created by the Duffer Brothers. Cast included Winona Ryder, David Harbour, Millie Bobby Brown, Finn Wolfhard, Noah Schnapp. The 2022 season 4 episode "Running Up That Hill" pushed Kate Bush's 1985 single to #1 in the UK, 37 years after its original release.

events.title: Scuttling of the Graf Spee
events.blurb: A feared commerce-raider that had sunk nine merchant ships in three months limped into a neutral harbour for repairs after a running battle with three smaller cruisers, then sat immobile while international diplomacy set a 72-hour countdown. Twenty thousand spectators lined the waterfront to watch her captain make his final decision.
events.revealBlurb: December 17, 1939, Montevideo. Captain Hans Langsdorff scuttled the Admiral Graf Spee at 8:55 PM rather than risk his crew in what he believed was an overwhelming British trap. Three days later he wrapped himself in the ship's battle ensign and shot himself. The trap was largely bluff.

events.title: Fall of Tobruk
events.blurb: A fortified port city that had withstood a nine-month siege the previous year fell to an armoured assault in a single day, yielding 33,000 prisoners — including an entire South African division — along with 2,000 vehicles, 5,000 tons of food, and enough fuel to sustain the attacking force's advance for weeks.
events.revealBlurb: June 21, 1942. Churchill learned of Tobruk's fall while meeting Roosevelt in Washington — handed a pink slip of paper mid-meeting. Roosevelt's immediate response: "What can we do to help?" He arranged 300 Sherman tanks and 100 self-propelled guns for immediate shipment. The news triggered a no-confidence vote against Churchill in the House of Commons.

events.title: Battle of Stalingrad
events.blurb: For six months, a city named after a living leader was fought over house by house, factory floor by factory floor, in temperatures reaching minus 40 degrees, as an encircled attacking force slowly starved and froze while its commander received a field marshal's baton and an order never to surrender. The first capitulation of an entire German field army in the war followed 12 days later.
events.revealBlurb: August 1942 – February 2, 1943. Of the 330,000 who entered the Stalingrad pocket, 91,000 surrendered — including 24 generals and Field Marshal Friedrich Paulus. Fewer than 6,000 of those prisoners ever returned to Germany. Hitler promoted Paulus to Field Marshal the day before surrender, noting no German field marshal had ever been taken alive.

events.title: Allied Invasion of Sicily
events.blurb: The largest amphibious operation to that point in military history put 160,000 troops, 3,000 ships, and 4,000 aircraft onto a Mediterranean island in a single night and day — opening the Allied campaign on the European continent itself and within three weeks causing the arrest and removal of a dictator who had held power for two decades.
events.revealBlurb: July 9–10, 1943 — Operation Husky. Benito Mussolini was deposed by his own Fascist Grand Council on July 25, just two weeks after the landings. An elaborate Allied deception operation, "Operation Mincemeat," had planted false documents on a corpse washed ashore in Spain suggesting the real target was Greece — and the Germans believed it.

events.title: Trinity Atomic Test
events.blurb: Scientists detonated a plutonium device atop a 30-metre steel tower in a remote desert basin before dawn, producing a fireball seen 250 miles away, a shockwave felt 100 miles away, and a mushroom cloud rising 12 kilometres into the sky — proving that a new class of weapon with the destructive power of 18,600 tons of TNT was now a practical reality.
events.revealBlurb: July 16, 1945 at 5:29:45 AM Mountain War Time, Jornada del Muerto desert, New Mexico. Witnessing the blast, project director J. Robert Oppenheimer recalled a line from the Bhagavad Gita: "Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds." Test director Kenneth Bainbridge's assessment was more blunt: "Now we are all sons of bitches."

events.title: Gallic Sack of Rome
events.blurb: Senone Gauls under their chieftain Brennus routed a Roman army at the Allia River, then entered a largely deserted Rome three days later and burned it for seven months. The sole holdout was the Capitoline Hill, where a sacred flock of geese allegedly woke the defenders when a Gallic night-assault crept up the cliffs.
events.revealBlurb: July 390 BCE, traditional (Polybius says 387). The ransom Brennus demanded in gold was agreed, but the Romans protested he was using rigged weights. Brennus reportedly threw his sword onto the scales and bellowed "Vae victis" — "Woe to the vanquished."

events.title: Licinian-Sextian Laws
events.blurb: After a decade of plebeian obstruction that left Rome with no consuls at all, the tribunes Gaius Licinius Stolo and Lucius Sextius Lateranus forced through three laws: one relieving debt, one limiting landholding to 500 iugera, and one requiring that at least one consul each year be a plebeian. Lucius Sextius duly became the first plebeian consul in 366 BCE.
events.revealBlurb: 367 BCE, Rome. Licinius and Sextius blocked every other piece of legislation for ten straight years to force the patricians to negotiate — essentially inventing the political hostage tactic of governmental gridlock.

events.title: Great Fire of Rome
events.blurb: A fire that broke out near the Circus Maximus burned for nine days and destroyed or severely damaged ten of Rome's fourteen districts, leaving the majority of the population homeless. Emperor Nero, who was at Antium when the fire started, blamed the city's small Christian community and launched the first state-sanctioned persecution of Christians in Roman history.
events.revealBlurb: July 18, 64 CE. The story that Nero fiddled while Rome burned is almost certainly false — the fiddle didn't exist yet, and multiple sources place him outside the city at the time. Tacitus, writing fifty years later, noted that many Romans suspected Nero ordered the fire himself but that the charge was never proven.

events.title: Theodosius Makes Christianity the Sole Legal Religion
events.blurb: Emperor Theodosius issued a series of decrees that outlawed public pagan sacrifice, closed all temples, extinguished the sacred fire of Vesta, disbanded the Vestal Virgins, and ended the Olympic Games. Christianity, which had been a persecuted sect three generations earlier, was now the only lawful religion of the Roman Empire.
events.revealBlurb: 391 CE. The Olympic Games, which had run continuously for over a thousand years, ended because Theodosius considered them a pagan festival — they were not revived until 1896. The fire of Vesta had burned in the Forum for centuries; snuffing it out was treated as a rupture with Rome's foundational identity.

events.title: Deposition of Romulus Augustulus
events.blurb: The Germanic warlord Odoacer deposed the sixteen-year-old emperor Romulus Augustulus at Ravenna — a boy whose mocking nickname meant "Little Augustus" — and sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople, informing the eastern emperor that the west no longer needed a separate ruler. Odoacer spared Romulus's life, finding him too young and too minor to bother executing, and exiled him to a villa in Campania on a pension.
events.revealBlurb: September 4, 476 CE. The last western emperor's name combined the city's legendary founder and its first emperor — an irony Roman writers noticed immediately. Contemporaries did not regard this moment as "the fall of Rome"; that framing came centuries later. The eastern empire in Constantinople continued for another 977 years.

events.title: Seneca Falls Convention
events.blurb: Three hundred people, a third of them men, gathered for two days at a Methodist chapel in upstate New York for the first women's rights convention held in the United States. Participants approved a "Declaration of Sentiments" modelled on the Declaration of Independence, demanding legal equality in marriage, property, education, employment, and the franchise. Only one resolution — women's suffrage — passed by a narrow vote.
events.revealBlurb: July 19-20, 1848 — Seneca Falls, NY. Lead organizers Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott. Only one signer, 19-year-old Charlotte Woodward, lived to vote in a federal election 72 years later. She was 91 and bed-ridden on Election Day 1920 and could not make it to the polls.

events.title: New Zealand Grants Women's Suffrage
events.blurb: The governor of a British colony in the South Pacific gave royal assent to an electoral act adding "and women" to the existing definition of qualified voters, making the colony the first self-governing country in the world to grant women the national franchise. Roughly 90,000 women registered within weeks; 82 percent of them turned out for the first subsequent election.
events.revealBlurb: September 19, 1893 — campaigners including Kate Sheppard delivered a petition a quarter of a kilometre long with nearly 32,000 signatures. The date is now Suffrage Day in New Zealand. Sheppard appears on the country's ten-dollar note.

events.title: 19th Amendment Ratified
events.blurb: Seven decades after a convention in upstate New York had narrowly resolved that women ought to vote, a Tennessee state legislator cast the deciding vote for his state's ratification — after reading a telegram from his mother urging him to do so. Women across the United States gained the national vote in time for the November presidential election, in which 8 million new voters participated.
events.revealBlurb: August 18, 1920 — the deciding vote was cast by Harry T. Burn, age 24. His mother's letter read: "Hurrah, and vote for suffrage. Don't keep them in doubt." The amendment was certified on August 26, now Women's Equality Day.

events.title: First Woman Prime Minister
events.blurb: The widow of an assassinated South Asian island-nation prime minister was sworn in as his successor, becoming the first woman to lead a national government anywhere in the world. She had entered politics only after her husband's murder the previous year. She would serve three separate terms over four decades, dying in office at age 84.
events.revealBlurb: July 21, 1960 — Sirimavo Bandaranaike of Ceylon (now Sri Lanka). She led a non-aligned left-of-center government; her daughter Chandrika became president 34 years later. She died on November 13, 2000, after casting her vote in a general election.

events.title: Margaret Thatcher Becomes PM
events.blurb: The leader of the British Conservative Party, a grocer's daughter who had studied chemistry at Oxford and later trained as a barrister, was invited by the monarch to form a government after her party won a sweeping parliamentary majority. She became the United Kingdom's first woman prime minister and would hold the office for 11 years — the longest continuous premiership of the 20th century.
events.revealBlurb: May 4, 1979 — she took office quoting St. Francis of Assisi on the doorstep: "Where there is discord, may we bring harmony." The next decade would be anything but that. She was forced to resign by her own cabinet in November 1990.

events.title: Trinity Nuclear Test
events.blurb: A plutonium implosion device was detonated atop a 30-metre steel tower in the New Mexico desert, producing a fireball visible 160 kilometres away and an explosion equivalent to 21 kilotons of TNT. Watching from a bunker 16 kilometres distant, the project's scientific director later recalled a verse from Hindu scripture about becoming death, destroyer of worlds.

events.title: People's Republic of China Proclaimed
events.blurb: Standing above a vast plaza in the Chinese capital, a revolutionary leader announced the founding of a new communist state after two decades of civil war and foreign occupation. His defeated nationalist rival retreated to an island 160 kilometres off the mainland coast and established a rival regime that persists today.
events.revealBlurb: October 1, 1949 — Mao Zedong declared the PRC from the Tiananmen gate. Chiang Kai-shek fled to Taiwan with 2 million refugees and most of the mainland's gold reserves. The split still defines East Asian geopolitics.

events.title: Julius and Ethel Rosenberg Executed
events.blurb: Julius and Ethel Rosenberg were executed by electric chair at Sing Sing Prison, having been convicted of passing atomic bomb design secrets to the Soviet Union — making them the only American civilians executed for espionage during the Cold War. Their case divided the nation, with their guilt debated in editorial pages, union halls, and diplomatic cables around the world.
events.revealBlurb: June 19, 1953 — Ossining, New York. Ethel Rosenberg required three jolts of electricity before she died; Julius was pronounced dead after the first. Subsequent release of Soviet archives confirmed Julius was a spy; historians still debate the extent of Ethel's involvement.

events.title: Suez Crisis
events.blurb: Britain, France, and Israel invaded Egypt to seize the nationalized waterway linking the Mediterranean to the Red Sea. The military operation succeeded; the political one did not. Under combined U.S. and Soviet pressure, the invaders withdrew within two months. The affair is remembered as the moment Britain stopped being a great power.
events.revealBlurb: October 29 to November 7, 1956 — Eisenhower was furious he hadn't been consulted and threatened to sell US holdings of British sterling. British PM Anthony Eden resigned in disgrace three months later. Nasser emerged as the hero of the Arab world.

events.title: Moscow Olympics Boycott
events.blurb: Sixty-six nations, led by the United States, refused to send athletes to the Summer Games held in the Soviet capital, protesting the invasion of a neighboring country five months earlier. Eighty nations competed anyway — the smallest field since 1956. Four years later, the Soviet bloc returned the favor by boycotting the Los Angeles Games.
events.revealBlurb: July 19, 1980 — the boycott was announced by Jimmy Carter. British athletes defied their own government and competed under the Olympic flag. The 1984 Soviet retaliation cost American sprinter Evelyn Ashford a likely gold-medal duel.

events.title: First Spacewalk
events.blurb: Soviet cosmonaut Alexei Leonov floated outside Voskhod 2 through an inflatable airlock and spent 12 minutes and 9 seconds in open space — the first human extravehicular activity. His spacesuit then ballooned in the vacuum to the point where he could no longer fit back through the hatch, forcing him to bleed pressure from a valve before squeezing inside headfirst.
events.revealBlurb: March 18, 1965 — Voskhod 2. The suit's engineers had fitted it with a built-in suicide pill. Leonov later said sweat filled his boots to the knee from the exertion of forcing himself back in. The spacecraft also drifted into an unplanned orbit and landed 386 km off target in the Ural mountains, where the crew spent a night in wolf country.

events.title: First Mars Close-Up Flyby
events.blurb: Mariner 4 flew within 9,846 km of Mars and transmitted 21 photographs covering about 1% of the planet's surface — the first close-range images of another planet. The images revealed a cratered, Moon-like landscape and showed Mars had a much thinner atmosphere than expected, with a surface pressure of roughly 4–7 millibars, dashing hopes of a habitable world.
events.revealBlurb: July 14, 1965 — Mariner 4. The images took four days to receive and were so eagerly anticipated that JPL technicians printed the first strips of data by hand onto paper using artist's pastels, coloring by number before the computer could process the file. The result was a blurry colored rectangle they pinned to a bulletin board.

events.title: Lunar Surface Landing
events.blurb: A spacecraft descended onto the Sea of Tranquility with 25 seconds of fuel remaining after the landing computer triggered five 1202 alarms caused by executive overflow. Two crew members spent 2 hours 31 minutes on the surface, collecting 21.5 kg of rock and soil and deploying a seismometer and a retroreflector array.
events.revealBlurb: July 20, 1969 — Apollo 11. Armstrong's first step came at 10:56 PM Eastern. The descent stage still sits on the Moon; the flag was knocked flat by the liftoff exhaust. The line was supposed to be "one small step for a man" — the transmission dropped the article, and Armstrong spent decades insisting he said it.

events.title: First American Woman in Space
events.blurb: Physicist Sally Ride flew aboard Space Shuttle Challenger as a mission specialist on STS-7, becoming the first American woman and the youngest American in space at 32. The six-day mission deployed two communications satellites and was the first shuttle flight to use a robotic arm to retrieve a free-flying satellite.
events.revealBlurb: June 18, 1983 — STS-7. A reporter asked Ride before launch whether spaceflight would affect her reproductive organs; she deadpanned that no one had asked her male crewmates the same question. NASA engineers reportedly asked whether 100 tampons would be enough for the six-day flight "just to be safe." She flew again in 1984 and co-founded a science education company.

events.title: Water Confirmed on the Moon
events.blurb: India's Chandrayaan-1 Moon Impact Probe detected spectral signatures consistent with water molecules during its 25-minute controlled descent to the lunar south pole, with readings from a mass spectrometer increasing steadily as the probe flew toward higher latitudes. Three instruments on the orbiting spacecraft corroborated the finding, confirming that water ice is present across the lunar surface.
events.revealBlurb: November 14, 2008 — Chandrayaan-1/MIP. The probe was decorated with the Indian national flag and crashed intentionally near Shackleton Crater at 85° south — making India the fourth nation to place an object on the Moon. The water discovery reversed decades of scientific consensus that the Moon was bone dry, reshaping plans for every future lunar base concept.

events.title: Indian Rebellion of 1857
events.blurb: Sepoys of the East India Company's Bengal Army, enraged by rumours that their rifle cartridges had been greased with beef and pork fat, rose in mutiny at a garrison town north of Delhi, shot their British officers, and marched south to proclaim a reluctant Mughal emperor the leader of a broader uprising. The revolt spread across north and central India over the following year.
events.revealBlurb: May 10, 1857 — Meerut. Bahadur Shah Zafar, the 82-year-old titular Mughal, was dragged out of retirement as figurehead. The revolt's brutal suppression ended Company rule in 1858; the British Crown took direct control of India.

events.title: Indian Independence & Partition
events.blurb: At the stroke of midnight, two new independent dominions came into existence on the subcontinent — one majority-Hindu, one majority-Muslim — as the British flag was lowered on the largest and oldest of Britain's imperial possessions. The division of provinces along religious lines displaced between 10 and 20 million people, and perhaps a million died in the communal violence that followed.
events.revealBlurb: August 14-15, 1947 — Pakistan on the 14th, India on the 15th. The boundary lines had been drawn by a London barrister, Cyril Radcliffe, who had never visited the subcontinent and had 36 days to complete the task. Nehru's "Tryst with Destiny" speech was delivered at midnight from the Constituent Assembly.

events.title: Economic Liberalization
events.blurb: Facing a balance-of-payments crisis so acute that the country had airlifted 47 tonnes of its gold reserves to London as collateral, a new finance minister presented a budget that systematically dismantled the license-permit-quota economy that had governed Indian business for four decades. Industrial licensing was abolished, imports liberalized, foreign investment welcomed. The economy would nearly quintuple over the next two decades.
events.revealBlurb: July 24, 1991 — Finance Minister Manmohan Singh's budget speech. Prime Minister Narasimha Rao provided the political cover. Singh, invoking Victor Hugo, declared: "No power on Earth can stop an idea whose time has come."

events.title: Kargil War
events.blurb: Pakistani soldiers, disguised as local insurgents, occupied high-altitude ridges inside the Indian-administered portion of a disputed northern territory over the winter. Their discovery by a shepherd in early May touched off a 74-day war fought at elevations up to 5,600 metres. India retook the peaks one by one with heavy infantry losses; Pakistan, pressured by Washington, withdrew.
events.revealBlurb: May 3 to July 26, 1999 — the Line of Control in Kargil, Ladakh. The conflict was one of the first televised wars in India. Captain Vikram Batra became a national hero before dying on Point 4875 on July 7.

events.title: 26/11 Mumbai Attacks
events.blurb: Ten men trained by a Pakistan-based militant group landed at a fishing harbour in the country's financial capital by rubber dinghy after hijacking an Indian fishing trawler at sea, and fanned out across the city to attack a railway station, a Jewish centre, a café, and two luxury hotels. The resulting sieges lasted 60 hours. 166 people died and more than 300 were wounded. Nine attackers were killed; the sole survivor was captured, tried, and hanged four years later.
events.revealBlurb: November 26-29, 2008 — Mumbai. The captured gunman, Ajmal Kasab, was hanged on November 21, 2012. The attacks were coordinated over satellite phone from Karachi; the operational planner, Sajid Mir, was finally convicted in Pakistan in 2022.

events.title: Vesalius Publishes De Fabrica
events.blurb: A 28-year-old Flemish anatomist at the University of Padua published a lavishly illustrated seven-volume atlas of human anatomy based on dissections he had performed personally, often on the bodies of recently executed criminals. Many of the 273 woodcut illustrations contradicted established Galenic teachings on points ranging from the structure of the jawbone to the absence of a hole between the heart's chambers. The book launched anatomy as a modern evidence-based science.
events.revealBlurb: 1543 — Andreas Vesalius, "De Humani Corporis Fabrica." The illustrations were probably drawn by students of Titian. Vesalius' enemies in traditional medical faculties fought him bitterly; he burned his own unpublished work in despair at one point and entered court life, dying on a pilgrimage 21 years later.

events.title: Banting Discovers Insulin
events.blurb: A 29-year-old Canadian surgeon and a 22-year-old graduate student, working in a borrowed University of Toronto lab through a hot summer, isolated an extract from dog pancreases that, when injected into diabetic dogs, brought their blood sugar back toward normal. By January of the following year, they had injected a 14-year-old boy dying of diabetes; he recovered dramatically. Diabetes, previously a death sentence for type 1 patients, became a manageable chronic disease.
