events.revealBlurb: July 27, 1921 — Frederick Banting and Charles Best. Banting and mentor John Macleod shared the 1923 Nobel; Banting split his prize money with Best. The team sold the patent rights to the University of Toronto for one dollar each. Insulin remains a life-saving medication for tens of millions.

events.title: First Successful Organ Transplant
events.blurb: A Boston surgical team performed the first successful kidney transplant, grafting a kidney donated by a healthy 23-year-old into his identical twin, who had been dying of chronic nephritis. The donor-recipient genetic match avoided rejection in an era before immunosuppressive drugs existed. The recipient lived eight more years; the donor lived another 56. The operation established organ transplantation as a viable medical field.
events.revealBlurb: December 23, 1954 — Joseph Murray at Peter Bent Brigham Hospital, Boston. Donor: Ronald Herrick. Recipient: Richard Herrick. Murray won the 1990 Nobel Prize in Medicine. Cyclosporine, the immunosuppressive that would permit non-related transplants, was not discovered until the 1970s.

events.title: Salk Polio Vaccine
events.blurb: The University of Michigan School of Public Health announced that the 40-year-old Pittsburgh virologist's killed-virus polio vaccine — tested the previous year on 1.8 million children in the largest medical trial then conducted — was "safe, effective, and potent." Polio, which had paralyzed 57,000 American children in 1952, became a preventable disease overnight. Millions wept in the streets. The vaccine's developer was offered a patent; he famously refused.
events.revealBlurb: April 12, 1955 — Jonas Salk. Edward R. Murrow asked him who owned the patent; he answered: "Well, the people, I would say. There is no patent. Could you patent the sun?" The Sabin oral vaccine, using live attenuated virus, arrived 1961 and became the standard globally.

events.title: First Test-Tube Baby
events.blurb: A baby girl was delivered by caesarean section at a Lancashire hospital — the first human born via in vitro fertilization. Her conception had involved an egg retrieved from her mother, fertilized in a laboratory dish, and implanted in the uterus nine years after the research team had first proposed the technique. The birth prompted intense ethical debate and religious protest. By 2020, about 1 percent of the world's babies were born via IVF.
events.revealBlurb: July 25, 1978 — Louise Brown at Oldham General Hospital. Pioneers: Robert Edwards, Patrick Steptoe, Jean Purdy. Edwards won the Nobel Prize in 2010 at age 85; Steptoe and Purdy had died. Brown herself had a second son born naturally in 2013.

events.title: Walden Published
events.blurb: A 37-year-old Massachusetts essayist, graduate of Harvard, former schoolteacher, and occasional pencil-factory worker, published an account of two years and two months he had spent living in a cabin he had built himself beside a glacier-pond near Concord. The book mixed natural observation, economic criticism, and philosophical reflection. It sold slowly; its reputation grew after the author's early death seven years later, and he is now considered one of the founders of American nature writing.
events.revealBlurb: August 9, 1854 — Henry David Thoreau. He had lived at Walden Pond 1845-47. The pond was, contrary to legend, a short walk from his family home; his mother did his laundry. Thoreau's civil-disobedience essay would later inspire Gandhi and Martin Luther King Jr.

events.title: Treasure Island Published
events.blurb: A 33-year-old Scottish writer, suffering severe pulmonary illness and convalescing in the Scottish Highlands, sketched a treasure map with his 12-year-old stepson on a rainy afternoon and began improvising a story for the boy. The serialized pirate adventure novel that grew from the map — featuring a peg-legged cook, a squawking parrot, a buried fortune, and a black spot — essentially defined the iconography of piracy for the next century and a half.
events.revealBlurb: November 14, 1883 — Robert Louis Stevenson. Initially serialized in the magazine Young Folks in 1881 as "The Sea Cook." The phrase "Shiver me timbers!" does not appear in the book but was popularized by its Long John Silver.

events.title: Rabindranath Tagore Wins Nobel
events.blurb: A 52-year-old Bengali polymath — poet, novelist, philosopher, composer, painter — was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature, becoming the first non-European and the first Asian to receive the honour. The Swedish Academy specifically cited his English translation of his own Bengali poetry collection "Gitanjali." The award brought him international fame; at home in colonial India it cemented him as a national cultural figure.
events.revealBlurb: November 13, 1913 — Rabindranath Tagore. He renounced his British knighthood in 1919 after the Jallianwala Bagh Massacre. He composed the national anthems of both India ("Jana Gana Mana") and Bangladesh ("Amar Shonar Bangla"), two of three anthems he wrote for different countries.

events.title: The Catcher in the Rye Published
events.blurb: A 32-year-old reclusive American short-story writer published his first and only novel, a 277-page first-person monologue narrated by a 16-year-old prep-school dropout wandering around Manhattan over three days in deep emotional distress. Critical reception was mixed; high-school teachers eventually banned and then assigned it across the country. The author retreated to rural New Hampshire and refused to publish again for decades.
events.revealBlurb: July 16, 1951 — J. D. Salinger. He died in 2010; only a handful of uncollected stories have emerged since. The novel was carried by Mark Chapman, who used it to explain killing John Lennon; by John Hinckley Jr., who attempted to assassinate Reagan; and by Robert Bardo, who killed actress Rebecca Schaeffer.

events.title: To Kill a Mockingbird Published
events.blurb: A 34-year-old Alabama-born New York airline reservation clerk published her first and, for over half a century, only novel — a semi-autobiographical story narrated by a six-year-old white girl whose father, a small-town Southern lawyer, defends a Black man falsely accused of raping a white woman. The book won a Pulitzer the next year and has been a school-curriculum fixture in the U.S. ever since.
events.revealBlurb: July 11, 1960 — Harper Lee. Her childhood friend Truman Capote was the model for the character Dill. Gregory Peck won an Oscar for the film adaptation. Lee published a second novel, "Go Set a Watchman," in 2015, a year before her death; it was an earlier draft of the same book.

events.title: Parthenon Completed
events.blurb: A marble temple dedicated to the patron goddess of an Athenian acropolis was completed after fifteen years of work. The structure refined classical Doric proportions, incorporated subtle optical corrections (all its columns lean slightly inward, curved "entasis" swelling their shafts) so the temple appears perfectly rectilinear from a distance, and housed a 12-metre ivory-and-gold statue of Athena. It stood substantially intact for over 2,000 years until a Venetian shell hit a Turkish powder magazine inside it in 1687.
events.revealBlurb: 438 BCE — Ictinus and Callicrates, architects, under Phidias as sculptor. Built on the acropolis of Athens under Pericles. The Elgin Marbles, sold to the British Museum in 1816, are fragments of the Parthenon's sculptural programme — still the subject of Greek repatriation demands.

events.title: Dome of the Rock Completed
events.blurb: An Umayyad caliph completed an octagonal Islamic shrine on the Temple Mount of a holy city, sheltering a rock Muslims believe the prophet Muhammad ascended to heaven from. Its distinctive gilded dome, 20 metres across, shimmered over the Old City; its interior walls were covered in Byzantine-style mosaics in golden, green, and blue. It is the oldest extant Islamic building and one of the earliest examples of monumental Islamic architecture.
events.revealBlurb: 691 CE — Caliph Abd al-Malik in Jerusalem. Built on the Noble Sanctuary, also the site of the ancient Jewish Second Temple. The gilded dome has been re-gilded many times; the current covering, added in 1993, used 80 kilograms of gold donated by King Hussein of Jordan.

events.title: Machu Picchu Built
events.blurb: An Inca emperor's royal estate was built at 2,430 metres on a narrow mountain ridge above a river in the Andes, with 200 stone buildings — agricultural terraces, palaces, temples — arranged on a mountain site that seemed intended for dramatic rather than practical reasons. It was abandoned roughly a century later for unclear reasons, possibly connected to the Spanish conquest of the Inca. The site remained unknown to the Spanish and, largely, to the outside world until 1911.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1450 — emperor Pachacuti. The American explorer Hiram Bingham encountered it on July 24, 1911. Local farmers had never really forgotten it; the "rediscovery" was primarily for outside audiences. It is now one of the New Seven Wonders of the World.

events.title: St. Paul's Cathedral Completed
events.blurb: After 35 years of construction replacing a medieval cathedral destroyed in the Great Fire of London, a 68-year-old English architect watched his son install the final piece of his new cathedral's lantern atop its dome — the first cathedral anywhere in the world to have been entirely designed, built, and completed by a single architect within his own lifetime. The triple-domed design, inspired by St. Peter's in Rome, rose 111 metres above the City of London.
events.revealBlurb: 1710 — Sir Christopher Wren. He also designed 52 other London churches after the Great Fire of 1666. He was buried in the cathedral's crypt when he died in 1723 at 90; his memorial reads "Si monumentum requiris, circumspice" — if you seek his monument, look around you.

events.title: Brooklyn Bridge Opens
events.blurb: The longest suspension bridge in the world — 486 metres between its Gothic granite towers — opened to foot and carriage traffic linking Manhattan and Brooklyn across the East River. Its construction had taken 14 years and cost 27 lives. The chief engineer had been paralyzed by decompression sickness while supervising caisson work; his wife Emily had effectively managed the final decade of the project from notes dictated in his sickroom.
events.revealBlurb: May 24, 1883 — designed by John A. Roebling (who died from a dockside accident early in construction). His son Washington Roebling suffered caisson disease and was bedridden; daughter-in-law Emily Warren Roebling led onsite engineering management. She was the first person to cross the completed bridge, in a carriage carrying a rooster.

events.title: Atari 2600 Launches
events.blurb: For the first time, a home console used interchangeable cartridges — meaning the same hardware could play a new game every week. Atari sold 250,000 units in the first months at $199 apiece. Within three years the living room had replaced the arcade as the primary venue for video games.
events.revealBlurb: September 11, 1977 — Atari released the Video Computer System (renamed 2600 in 1982). By 1982, 15 million 2600s had been sold and the console was generating $2 billion in annual revenue.

events.title: Space Invaders Hits Japanese Arcades
events.blurb: An alien formation that descended one row lower every time a column was destroyed — a quirk of the hardware clock — accidentally created the defining tension mechanic of arcade games. The game was so popular in Japan that bars converted into dedicated parlours.
events.revealBlurb: July 1978 — Taito released Space Invaders in Japan. The Atari 2600 home port in 1980 quadrupled console sales that year. The "yen coin shortage" is an urban legend — numismatists have found no evidence in mint records.

events.title: Asteroids Released by Atari
events.blurb: Drawing lines on a vector monitor to simulate drifting through space debris sounds modest. The game that resulted became Atari's best-selling arcade cabinet of all time, pulling in an estimated 10 million quarters per day at its peak. Demand was so extreme that Atari temporarily halted production of other games and shipped Asteroids units inside Lunar Lander cabinets just to get them out the door faster.
events.revealBlurb: November 1979 — Atari released Asteroids in North American arcades. It sold over 70,000 cabinets. The game's high score table was the first widely adopted public performance metric in gaming — and the first subject of documented high-score fraud.

events.title: Nintendo Game Boy Launches in North America
events.blurb: Competing handhelds boasted colour screens and better hardware. Nintendo shipped a grey brick with a pea-green LCD and bundled it with a Soviet puzzle game about falling tetrominoes. The grey brick won. Within weeks every unit in the United States had sold out.
events.revealBlurb: July 31, 1989 — The Game Boy launched in North America at $89.99, selling 40,000 units on day one. The Game Boy line eventually sold 118 million units. The Japan launch had been April 21, 1989.

events.title: Oculus Rift Kickstarter Campaign Launches
events.blurb: A 19-year-old in his parents' garage had spent years building virtual reality headsets from scavenged parts. His Kickstarter campaign asked for $250,000 to build a developer kit. It raised $2.4 million from nearly 10,000 backers. Two years later, Facebook acquired his company for $2 billion.
events.revealBlurb: August 1, 2012 — Palmer Luckey launched the Oculus Rift Kickstarter, raising 974% of its $250,000 goal. Facebook (now Meta) acquired Oculus VR in March 2014 for approximately $2 billion.

events.title: Military Desegregation Order
events.blurb: A U.S. president signed an executive order mandating "equality of treatment and opportunity" in the armed forces without regard to race, color, religion, or national origin. The army resisted for nearly five years; full integration of combat units was not achieved until the Korean War made ignoring Black replacements impossible.
events.revealBlurb: July 26, 1948 — Executive Order 9981, Harry Truman. He signed it partly out of conviction, partly because Black voters in northern cities were now pivotal to Democratic victory. The last all-Black unit was dissolved in 1954.

events.title: March on Washington
events.blurb: A quarter-million Americans — three-quarters Black, a quarter white — gathered between the Washington and Lincoln Memorials on the 100th anniversary summer of the Emancipation Proclamation to demand the passage of civil-rights legislation then stalled in Congress. The event's closing address, given on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial, contained a phrase repeated in eight paragraphs: "I have a dream."
events.revealBlurb: August 28, 1963. MLK's prepared text did not contain "I have a dream" — Mahalia Jackson, behind him on the dais, shouted "Tell them about the dream, Martin!" and he ad-libbed the most famous passage. The Justice Department had 4,000 troops on standby in case of violence. None was needed.

events.title: Bloody Sunday in Selma
events.blurb: Six hundred civil-rights marchers, demanding federal protection for Black voting rights, set out from a small Alabama city to walk 87 kilometres to the state capital. On the Edmund Pettus Bridge at the edge of town, state troopers and a sheriff's posse on horseback charged them with clubs and tear gas. Televised images of a beaten John Lewis shocked the nation into action.
events.revealBlurb: March 7, 1965 — Selma, Alabama. Lewis's skull was fractured. Lyndon Johnson appeared before a joint session of Congress eight days later to introduce the Voting Rights Act, closing with the movement's own anthem: "We shall overcome."

events.title: Thurgood Marshall Confirmed
events.blurb: The U.S. Senate confirmed the first African-American justice of the Supreme Court by a vote of 69-11 after a contentious hearing in which Southern senators grilled him on obscure constitutional questions in an effort to embarrass him. He had already argued 32 cases before the Court — and won 29 — as the NAACP's lead attorney. He served 24 years.
events.revealBlurb: August 30, 1967 — confirmed to replace Tom Clark. Lyndon Johnson had said bluntly on tape: "I want folks to look up and see a Negro lawyer up there." Marshall was the grandson of a slave and had been rejected by the University of Maryland law school on racial grounds.

events.title: MLK Day Signed
events.blurb: After 15 years of advocacy by civil rights leaders, Congress passed and the president signed legislation establishing the third Monday of January as a federal holiday honoring the slain civil rights leader. The fight to pass it had drawn bitter opposition from some senators, including one who conducted a 16-day filibuster. It became the first federal holiday commemorating an African-American.
events.revealBlurb: November 2, 1983 — Ronald Reagan. Arizona voters rejected recognizing the holiday in 1990; the NFL moved the 1993 Super Bowl from Phoenix in response, and the state reversed course. New Hampshire, the last holdout, adopted it in 1999.

events.title: First Soviet Atomic Bomb Test
events.blurb: Four years after U.S. weapons ended the Pacific war, Soviet scientists detonated their own plutonium implosion device at a test range in the Kazakh steppe. Western intelligence had predicted the breakthrough was at least five years away. The explosion ended the American nuclear monopoly and opened the arms race.
events.revealBlurb: August 29, 1949 — codename RDS-1, nicknamed "First Lightning." The design was largely cribbed from the U.S. Fat Man bomb via spy networks inside the Manhattan Project. Klaus Fuchs had handed over detailed blueprints.

events.title: Korean War Armistice
events.blurb: After three years and more than two million deaths, military commanders from three nations signed a ceasefire in a frontier village, establishing a 4-kilometre-wide demilitarized strip along the 38th parallel where fighting had essentially started. No peace treaty has ever been signed. The two Koreas remain technically at war.
events.revealBlurb: July 27, 1953 — signed at Panmunjom. The DMZ is now the most heavily mined place on Earth. Because no peace treaty followed, a single gunshot across the line could theoretically restart the war tomorrow.

events.title: Berlin Wall Built
events.blurb: Overnight, East German soldiers and workers unrolled barbed wire along the jagged frontier between the two halves of a divided city, cutting off the escape route that some 3.5 million people had used to flee west over the previous twelve years. Within days the wire was replaced with concrete. Families woke to find themselves permanently separated from relatives one street away.
events.revealBlurb: August 13, 1961 — construction began at 2 AM on a Sunday. The wall eventually grew to 155 kilometres, with 302 watchtowers and a "death strip" of raked sand and trip-wires. At least 140 people died trying to cross it going west.

events.title: Moscow-Washington Hotline
events.blurb: Shaken by how close they had come to nuclear war the previous October, the United States and Soviet Union signed a memorandum of understanding establishing a direct teleprinter link between their capitals. Contrary to Hollywood, it was never a red telephone — it was a clunky, secure teletype system. The first test message read: "THE QUICK BROWN FOX JUMPS OVER THE LAZY DOG."
events.revealBlurb: June 20, 1963 — signed in Geneva. The line was first used in earnest in 1967 during the Arab-Israeli War. Today it's a secure email system; neither side actually picks up a red phone.

events.title: Gulf of Tonkin Incident
events.blurb: A U.S. Navy destroyer reported it had been attacked by small torpedo boats off the North Vietnamese coast. Two nights later, the same destroyer and a second reported a second attack in bad weather — an attack that likely never happened. Within days, Congress passed a resolution authorizing the president to use "all necessary measures" in Southeast Asia, opening the door to full-scale war.
events.revealBlurb: August 2 and 4, 1964 — the second "attack" was almost certainly radar ghosts and jumpy sonar operators. The resolution passed the House 416-0 and the Senate 88-2. Declassified NSA documents in 2005 confirmed the fabrication.

events.title: Shaanxi Earthquake
events.blurb: The deadliest earthquake in recorded human history struck a densely populated region of northern China in the early morning, collapsing hillsides dotted with cave dwellings carved from soft loess soil. Roughly 830,000 people died — some 60 percent of the population of the affected counties. In some districts, everyone was killed.
events.revealBlurb: January 23, 1556 — Shaanxi Province, Ming Dynasty. The loess hillsides, prized for their insulation, became mass graves when the quake liquefied them. The toll remains a single-event record four and a half centuries later.

events.title: Tangshan Earthquake
events.blurb: A magnitude 7.6 earthquake struck a heavily industrialized city in northern China at 3:42 AM, when residents were asleep in masonry buildings that collapsed upon them. Official Chinese figures put the death toll at 242,000, but some estimates exceed 650,000. It is the second-deadliest earthquake of the 20th century.
events.revealBlurb: July 28, 1976 — Tangshan, Hebei Province. Mao Zedong, dying in Beijing, was briefly informed and reportedly wept. He died six weeks later; many traditional Chinese interpreters saw the quake as the Mandate of Heaven being withdrawn from his regime.

events.title: Deepwater Horizon Spill
events.blurb: A blowout on a semi-submersible drilling rig in the Gulf of Mexico killed 11 workers and severed the riser pipe to a well 1,500 metres below the surface. Over the next 87 days, as engineers tried increasingly improbable methods to cap it, roughly 780 million litres of crude oil gushed into the sea — the largest accidental marine oil spill in history.
events.revealBlurb: April 20, 2010 — off Louisiana. The well was finally killed in mid-September. BP paid over $65 billion in settlements, fines, and cleanup. A live-stream of the ocean-floor plume was watched by millions during the crisis; executives who claimed it was "relatively tiny" became memes.

events.title: COVID-19 Pandemic Declared
events.blurb: The World Health Organization, having watched a novel coronavirus spread from a single city to 114 countries in ten weeks, formally upgraded its assessment from epidemic to pandemic. Within days, much of the world entered some form of lockdown — schools shut, flights grounded, stock markets crashed. Before vaccines arrived a year later, it would kill millions.
events.revealBlurb: March 11, 2020 — WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus. The first known case had been reported in Wuhan in early December 2019. Official global death toll exceeded 7 million; excess mortality studies suggest the real number is closer to 20 million.

events.title: Beirut Port Explosion
events.blurb: 2,750 tonnes of ammonium nitrate that had been haphazardly stored in a warehouse at a Mediterranean capital's port for six years detonated after a smaller fire reached it. The blast was felt 240 kilometres away in Cyprus, killed 218 people, injured 7,000, and left 300,000 homeless. It ranks among the largest non-nuclear explosions ever recorded.
events.revealBlurb: August 4, 2020 — Beirut, Lebanon. The chemicals had been offloaded from a Russian ship in 2013 and simply abandoned. The blast crater was 124 metres wide. Years later no senior official has faced trial; the investigation has been repeatedly obstructed by politicians named as suspects.

events.title: MTV First Broadcast
events.blurb: A music video channel began broadcasting at 12:01 a.m., opening with a brief spoken introduction before playing a three-minute clip of a rock band performing against footage of a rocket launch. The first words spoken on air were "Ladies and gentlemen, rock and roll" — the channel ran continuously for 24 hours with no advertisements.

events.title: Prince Charles Marries Diana
events.blurb: The heir to the British throne, 32, married a 20-year-old shy nursery-school assistant at a grand ceremony at a London cathedral. The televised wedding drew 750 million viewers worldwide and unfolded like a fairytale: horse-drawn carriages, a 25-foot train on the bride's silk ivory dress, a balcony kiss at a royal palace afterward. The marriage itself would be miserable; the couple separated in 1992 and divorced in 1996. Both remarried others, and the bride died in a Paris car crash in 1997.
events.revealBlurb: July 29, 1981 — Charles, Prince of Wales and Lady Diana Spencer at St. Paul's Cathedral. Diana tripped on her father's name during the vows ("Philip Charles Arthur George" instead of "Charles Philip..."). Charles, now King Charles III, succeeded his mother Elizabeth II in September 2022.

events.title: Apple's "1984" Super Bowl Ad
events.blurb: A 60-second commercial produced by a British director for a California computer company aired during the third quarter of the Super Bowl. The ad showed a dystopian audience of grey workers watching a Big-Brother-like speaker on a vast screen; an athletic woman in running clothes smashed the screen with a hammer. The product was the Macintosh computer. Apple's board had voted to kill the ad; the CEO insisted it air. It aired once.
events.revealBlurb: January 22, 1984 — directed by Ridley Scott. The ad ran nationally only that one time; it has since been shown as a promotion or film-clip thousands of times. Macintosh sales in its first 100 days exceeded expectations. The "1984" ad is still considered one of the greatest commercials ever made.

events.title: Nintendo NES Released in US
events.blurb: A Japanese toy company launched, in a limited New York test market, a home video-game console — two years after it had flopped in its first US release attempt under the brand name Advanced Video System. The relaunched system came with a new console design, a "Zapper" light gun, a robotic companion, and a launch bundle including Super Mario Bros. The North American video game market had collapsed in 1983; the Nintendo relaunch is widely credited with reviving it.
events.revealBlurb: October 18, 1985 — Nintendo Entertainment System (NES). The Japanese original ("Famicom") had launched in July 1983. R.O.B. the robot's inclusion was marketing cleverness to avoid "video game" retailer resistance — the NES was pitched initially as a toy. By 1988, 7 million units had sold.

events.title: Nevermind Released
events.blurb: A three-piece rock band from Aberdeen, Washington released their second album featuring a swimming infant reaching for a dollar bill on a fishhook. Within three months it had displaced a reigning pop star's record from the top of the Billboard 200, and its lead single's music video received more plays on music television than any previous video.

events.title: Cyrus the Great Takes Babylon
events.blurb: A Persian king who had already conquered Media, Lydia, and the Ionian cities entered the ancient city of Babylon without a fight, claiming to have been welcomed by its priests as the rightful king of the gods. His subsequent proclamation — known from a surviving cuneiform cylinder — repatriated exiled populations, restored local temples, and is sometimes described as the oldest surviving charter of human rights. The Persian Achaemenid Empire he founded became the largest the world had yet seen.
events.revealBlurb: October 29, 539 BCE — Cyrus II. The Cyrus Cylinder is now in the British Museum. The Hebrew Bible credits Cyrus with allowing the Judean exiles to return to Jerusalem and rebuild the Temple; he is the only non-Jewish figure called "messiah" in the Hebrew scriptures.

events.title: First Punic War Begins
events.blurb: The Roman Republic and the Carthaginian Empire, the two rising powers of the western Mediterranean, went to war over control of a large island between them. The conflict would last 23 years and transform Rome from a purely land-based power into a naval one — the Romans, ignorant of shipbuilding, reportedly reverse-engineered a captured Carthaginian warship to build their first fleet. Rome eventually won and imposed a crushing indemnity; the seed of two more wars was planted.
events.revealBlurb: 264 BCE — Rome vs. Carthage over Sicily. "Punic" comes from the Latin for "Phoenician," Carthage's origin. The Romans invented boarding bridges ("corvi") that turned sea battles into quasi-land battles they could win. Rome lost 700 ships over the course of the war, mostly to storms.

events.title: Battle of Cannae
events.blurb: Hannibal's army of roughly 50,000 men destroyed a Roman force of 80,000 in a single afternoon by letting the Roman center push forward into a concave line, then closing cavalry on both flanks until the entire legionary mass was encircled and butchered. Between 55,000 and 70,000 Romans died; senators threw handfuls of gold rings stripped from dead equestrians into a bowl to show Carthage the scale of the slaughter.
events.revealBlurb: August 2, 216 BCE, Apulia. The double-envelopment Hannibal used at Cannae became the template studied at military academies for 2,000 years. Hannibal's war elephants, his most famous asset, had all died before this battle.

events.title: Destruction of the Second Temple
events.blurb: A Roman general's army of 70,000 legionaries, closing the siege of a rebellious Judean capital after a four-year Jewish revolt, breached the walls and burned the city's Second Temple on the anniversary of the first Temple's destruction 656 years earlier. The Temple was never rebuilt; a Western retaining wall remains the holiest site in Judaism. Roman troops hauled the Temple menorah and other sacred vessels to Rome, where a victory arch depicting the procession still stands.
events.revealBlurb: 70 CE — the siege was commanded by Titus, son of the emperor Vespasian. The Arch of Titus, completed c. 81 CE, still stands at the east end of the Roman Forum. The Western Wall is the most significant surviving fragment; Orthodox Jews mourn the Temple's destruction each year on Tisha B'Av.

events.title: Fall of Constantinople
events.blurb: An Ottoman sultan, 21 years old, directed a 53-day siege of the Byzantine capital with 80,000 troops, an army of miners who tunneled under the walls, and enormous bronze cannons that fired 550-kilogram stone balls. The last Roman emperor died fighting at a breach in his city's walls. The 1,100-year-old Byzantine state, the direct legal continuation of Roman rule, ended.
events.revealBlurb: May 29, 1453 — Mehmed II. The city's Greek name, Constantinople, stayed in formal Ottoman use until 1930; "Istanbul" is how Byzantine Greeks had always said "to the city" colloquially. Hagia Sophia became a mosque that Friday.

events.title: Raja Harishchandra Released
events.blurb: A mythological silent film about the legendarily truthful king Harishchandra — shot in Bombay using an all-male cast because no actress would agree to appear on screen — opened at the Coronation Cinematograph in Girgaon and became India's first feature film, running 3,700 feet of hand-cranked footage. Its creator had spent over a year learning to develop film himself after being refused laboratory access.
events.revealBlurb: May 3, 1913 — Dadasaheb Phalke's debut. He was a printer by trade. Legend says he watched The Life of Christ (1906) in Bombay and decided India needed its own screen mythology. All the female roles were played by male wrestlers and cooks; no respectable woman would work in pictures.

events.title: Bombay Talkies Founded
events.blurb: A studio established in Malad, Bombay, by a London-trained filmmaker and his aristocratic actress-wife drew European technical talent — German cameramen, British equipment — to build India's first modern film facility with synchronised sound stages and a Western-style star system. It launched the careers of Dilip Kumar, Ashok Kumar, and Madhubala within its first fifteen years.
events.revealBlurb: April 15, 1934 — founded by Himanshu Rai and Devika Rani. Rai died in 1940 while the studio was mid-production; Devika Rani, then 32, took sole control and ran it for another nine years. The studio was where a young Dilip Kumar walked in looking for work and was handed a contract he barely understood.

events.title: Mughal-e-Azam Released
events.blurb: A Mughal-court epic that took sixteen years to complete — halted twice by financial collapse and partitioned away from its original cast — cost ₹1.5 crore, more than any previous Indian film, and spent ₹1 crore on a single song filmed in a replica of the Sheesh Mahal built with imported Belgian glass. Released in black and white, it was the highest-grossing Indian film for fifteen years.
events.revealBlurb: August 5, 1960 — directed by K. Asif. The original Akbar died before filming could restart; the entire cast was rebuilt after Partition. In 2004 it became the first Indian black-and-white film to be digitally colourised and theatrically re-released — and was a commercial success all over again.

events.title: Hum Aapke Hain Koun..! Released
events.blurb: A fourteen-song, over-three-hour family wedding drama that critics pre-screened and privately predicted was an unreleasable disaster became, on release, the first Hindi film to gross ₹1 billion — selling 74 million tickets domestically, the highest footfall for any Hindi film since the 1990s. The industry pivoted overnight toward family-oriented, non-violent spectacle.
events.revealBlurb: August 5, 1994 — director Sooraj Barjatya, a sequel of sorts to his earlier Maine Pyar Kiya. Salman Khan and Madhuri Dixit were cast against type as wholesome leads. The film ran in a Mumbai multiplex for over three years without leaving screens.

events.title: Taare Zameen Par Released
events.blurb: A film about an eight-year-old with undiagnosed dyslexia shipped off to boarding school for failing every subject — told largely from the child's hallucinatory perspective — earned ₹98 crore worldwide and prompted school boards across India to introduce dyslexia screening. Its child lead, discovered through an open casting call, had never acted before.
events.revealBlurb: December 21, 2007 — Aamir Khan's directorial debut, having taken over from Amole Gupte mid-production. Darsheel Safary, then 9, auditioned among 1,000 children. The film catalysed new Indian legislation on learning disability accommodation in schools. Khan dedicated the film to every child who had been misunderstood.
